title: The Dalai Lamas
hookLine: the line of Dalai Lamas, and the Fifth, who unified Tibet

lines: A CHILD AND A TRAY OF OBJECTS.
cards: A small child in a farmhouse is shown a tray of objects: prayer beads, a walking stick, a small drum. Some belonged to a teacher who has died. Some did not.
The visitors who brought the tray are monks, and they're watching which ones the child reaches for. Stories like this are told about how a new teacher in a line is found.
One of these lines carries a title known far beyond Tibet.

teach.h: A TEACHER RECOGNIZED AGAIN: A TULKU.
teach.b: In Tibetan Buddhism, a great teacher who dies may be recognized again in a child, who is found, tested, trained, and then takes up the same work. Such a teacher is called a tulku.
The tradition holds that this happens out of compassion: a teacher chooses to come back to keep helping. The Dalai Lamas are one of these lines, in the Gelug school.
Tibetan Buddhists regard them as an emanation of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, whom Tibetans call Chenrezig.
So, Tibetans say, to honor a Dalai Lama is to honor compassion itself, wearing a human face.
Then the Fifth, often called the Great Fifth. In his time, Tibet was divided among rival rulers and rival schools.
With the help of a Mongol ruler who backed him, he came to lead a unified Tibetan government, as both its spiritual and its political head.
He was also a scholar and a writer, and he began the building we'll visit tomorrow. Honesty matters here.
Tibetan Buddhists hold the line as compassion at work, and it has also lived inside real history: alliances, wars, rival claims, hard choices. Tibetan histories tell it with many of those turns.
Holding both, the compassion and the politics, is part of telling it fairly.
The line continues today, each Dalai Lama counted by number, so each number carries the whole line behind it.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism, tulkus are searched for and recognized after a teacher's death, then raised and trained in a monastery; the Dalai Lamas belong to the Gelug school and are regarded as emanations of Avalokiteshvara, Chenrezig.

wait until the child is grown and ask.
games.why: stories tell of children shown a teacher's belongings mixed with others, and watched to see which they reach for.

practice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something, a teacher, a relative, someone who passed on a craft, and then, if you know it, the person who taught them, and say the two names silently, like beads on a string.
If no name comes, use Chenrezig, the name Tibetans give to compassion in bodhisattva form. Then rest, and let the breath be the thread.
